raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old woman with no known EBOV contact sought treatment at an Ebola isolation unit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, on January 1, 2015 (day 7 of illness). She was afebrile and weak, but ambulatory, with a history of fever, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and muscle and joint pain. According to local protocol, she was given oral antimalarial, antimicrobial, and antiemetic drugs and oral rehydration therapy. On day 8 of illness, after testing EBOV PCR-positive (cycle threshold [Ct] value of 23.5), she was given intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) for 7 days, artesunate (180 mg) for 3 days, and Ringer's lactate (4-6 L) with supplemental KCl for 5 days.
During days 13-15, the patient improved, moving independently and talking. On day 16, she became confused; by day 20, she was unresponsive to voices. Intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and artesunate (180 mg) were administered for an additional 7 and 3 days, respectively. On days 28 and 29, she was still unconscious; serum PCR test results on both days were negative for EBOV. On day 29, she was transferred to Connaught Hospital in Freetown, where she had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15 (E3, V1, M5) but no localizing or focal signs. She was given intravenous fluconazole (800 mg 1x/d). Admission blood test results showed anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase and C-reactive protein, and low creatinine (Technical Appendix). HIV test results were negative. 
On day 34, large-joint polyarthritis of the right shoulder, left elbow, and left knee developed. Affected joints appeared normal on radiographs, and synovial fluid (15 mL) from the left knee was EBOV PCR negative. She was given diclofenac (50 mg 2x/d) and 1 intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone (80 mg). Concurrent blood PCR on day 34 was negative.
By day 41 she was more alert, although her family reported she had slowed responses. Lumbar puncture was performed; opening pressure (30 cm H2O) was elevated, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 37.6), as determined by using the Public Health England in-house, optimized version of the Trombley assay with a cutoff Ct value of 40. Concurrent catheter specimens of urine and blood samples tested EBOV-negative. FilmArray (BioFire Diagnostics, Salt Lake City, UT, USA) testing showed methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae in CSF and mixed pathogens in urine. A computer tomographic scan image of the patient's head showed substantial cerebral atrophy without hydrocephalus (Figure).
On day 44, an underarm sweat swab sample was PCR-positive (Ct value 39.6) and a buccal swab sample PCR-negative for EBOV. Ongoing painful synovitis was treated with an additional 80-mg intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone. On day 51, a midstream urine sample was EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 35.7), and an underarm sweat swab sample was EBOV PCR-negative. The patient was discharged; her family was advised to minimize contact with her body fluids.
At follow-up on day 64, the patient's family reported she had impaired short-term memory and ongoing slowness. She had a score of 18/23 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, but general neurologic exam results were normal. A midstream urine test was still EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 39.6); PCR of her sweat swab sample was inhibited (Technical Appendix). She was referred to the local survivors' clinic; no contact cases were reported.
The depressed mental status and presence of EBOV in this case-patient's CSF are consistent with encephalitis, a finding in autopsies of persons with Marburg virus infection and in EBOV nonhuman primate models. The general atrophy seen in computer tomographic scan images is consistent with a rapidly developing complication of a diffuse inflammatory process. Given inadequate antimicrobial drug doses for meningitis and clinical improvement, we believe methicillin-resistant S. aureus and K. pneumoniae were CSF sample contaminants.
This case shows the brain's immune privilege is incomplete for EBOV and prompts a broader discussion regarding neurovirulence in Ebola virus disease. Our finding that EBOV can be present in CSF, even after serum clearance, adds to the knowledge of neurologic symptoms in acute infection and of postinfectious sequelae in observational clinical studies. This finding raises the possibility that EBOV persistence elsewhere in the body, or in multiple organs, could be an indicator of or risk for central nervous system invasion. 
Our report has limitations. We could not perform many blood chemistry tests, in-country virus cultures, or deep sequencing on samples. Likewise, diagnosis of coma was challenging because of the lack of CSF cell counts, biochemistry values, and paired EBOV IgG and IgM titers in CSF and blood.
This case raises the practical issue that Ebola treatment requires understanding of multiorgan virologic and inflammatory complications; survivor care and research programs should screen for neurocognitive impairment and consider appropriate imaging. The case confirms previously reported intermittent EBOV PCR positivity in urine. The development of arthritis with synovitis, treated with corticosteroids, supports the diagnosis of reactive arthritis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old female presenting with weakness, headache, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and generalized musculoskeletal pain for 7 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented on day 7 of illness to an isolation unit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, with a 7-day history of fever, nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, headache, and diffuse muscle and joint pain. Ambulatory and afebrile upon initial evaluation, she received empiric oral therapies. On day 8 of illness, she was initiated on intravenous antimicrobials and fluids. Between days 13 and 15, she showed clinical improvement, ambulating and vocalizing independently. On day 16, she developed acute confusion, progressing by day 20 to unresponsiveness. She remained comatose and on day 29 was transferred to Connaught Hospital. On day 34, she developed acute large-joint polyarthritis. By day 41, her sensorium improved with residual psychomotor slowing. At day 64 follow-up, she demonstrated short-term memory impairment and ongoing cognitive slowness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Freetown, Sierra Leone; denies known contact with individuals infected with viral hemorrhagic fever. No other prior medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, headache, generalized myalgia, arthralgia, profound weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Day 7 (initial presentation): afebrile and weak, but ambulatory. Day 29 (hospital admission): Glasgow Coma Scale 9/15 (E3 V1 M5), no focal neurological signs or localizing deficits. Day 34: large-joint polyarthritis with acute synovitis involving the right shoulder, left elbow, and left knee. Day 41: alert, with slowed verbal and motor responses. Day 64 (follow-up): Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score 18/23; cranial nerves and general neurological examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 29 blood tests: anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), and low serum creatinine. Rapid HIV antibody test: negative. Day 34 joint radiographs (right shoulder, left elbow, left knee): normal joint architecture without erosive or osseous abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 41 lumbar puncture: elevated CSF opening pressure of 30 cm H2O. CSF BioFire FilmArray: positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae (considered contaminants); urine FilmArray showed mixed flora. Non-contrast head CT: marked generalized cerebral atrophy without hydrocephalus. Day 34 left knee arthrocentesis: 15 mL of synovial fluid aspirated.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Ebola virus disease (EBOV) complicated by viral meningoencephalitis/CNS persistence and post-viral reactive arthritis: Blood RT-PCR positive for EBOV on day 8 (cycle threshold [Ct] 23.5). Subsequent blood RT-PCR assays negative on days 28, 29, and 34, confirming systemic clearance. CSF RT-PCR on day 41 positive for EBOV (Ct 37.6 via optimized Trombley assay; cutoff Ct 40). Concurrent blood and catheter urine samples on day 41 were EBOV-negative. Synovial fluid PCR on day 34 was EBOV-negative. Axillary sweat swab PCR was EBOV-positive on day 44 (Ct 39.6) and negative on day 51. Midstream urine PCR was EBOV-positive on day 51 (Ct 35.7) and day 64 (Ct 39.6). Antimicrobial and supportive therapy: Oral antimalarials, antimicrobials, antiemetics, and oral rehydration therapy upon arrival; intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 7 days (days 8-14) and repeated for 7 days (from day 20); intravenous artesunate 180 mg daily for 3 days (days 8-10) and repeated for 3 days (from day 20); Ringer's lactate 4-6 L daily with supplemental KCl for 5 days; intravenous fluconazole 800 mg once daily starting day 29. Reactive polyarthritis and painful synovitis treated with oral diclofenac 50 mg twice daily and two intramuscular doses of methylprednisolone 80 mg (days 34 and 44). Patient discharged on day 51 and referred to the local survivor clinic with residual neurocognitive impairment.
